title: The Revenge of Geography: What the Map Tells Us About Coming Conflicts and the Battle Against Fate
author: Robert D. Kaplan
vetoReason: Geographer Ron Johnston directly challenges the book's central reduction of geopolitical explanation to configuration, topography and distance, and its selective reliance on older thinkers while omitting contemporary political geography. The causal framework is the target, not a dispute about individual forecasts. The Population and Development Review critique independently finds the central claims unsupported by the descriptive evidence.
note: Mandatory Karpathy review and matching Subcritical Appraisal occurrence counted once each. Explanatory nonfiction passes hard gates. Kirkus and Harm de Blij praise its breadth and geographical insight; these defenses preserve counterfactual value. They do not remove the substantial critique of its recurring causal narrative. No single historical period: cases support contemporary geopolitical claims. Global scope prevents T11; geopolitics dominates T12. Not selected.
notes: Selected geography and historical cases do not adequately test competing causal explanations.
Links territory, resources, population, trade routes and military power.
Useful constraint questions, but application needs independent institutional and historical analysis.
Frequently moves from spatial conditions to political outcomes without sufficient causal discrimination.
D=6, moderate confidence from Johnston, de Blij and readers. Regional cases add facts; extended older-theory exposition and uneven maps limit learning yield.
Geographic constraints endure; particular strategic forecasts do not.
Geostrategy, resources and logistics fit partly, with power dominant.
Experienced field reporter, with strong criticism from disciplinary specialists.
Wide-ranging structure and vivid observations, but uneven accessibility.
Fluent language sometimes turns possibilities into necessities.

title: The War on Normal People: The Truth About America's Disappearing Jobs and Why Universal Basic Income Is Our Future
author: Andrew Yang
note: Mandatory Karpathy review. Policy argument with autobiographical material, not technical training. Introduction and contents center automation, employment and proposed institutions. Connection to a presidential campaign does not by itself establish dominant leader recruitment under V6. Crocker and Widerquist support its contribution to the basic-income debate; PW and Kirkus find diagnosis stronger than remedies. Forecasts are assessed as 2018 claims, not current facts. No high-confidence veto established from inspected evidence. US social policy dominates both thematic deductions. Not selected: policy advocacy and unsettled forecasts are less suitable than the strongest technical narratives.
notes: Documented social indicators mixed with uncertain displacement projections and policy assumptions.
Links automation, labor markets, regional decline, welfare and taxation.
Useful questions about distribution of productivity gains; prescriptions remain context dependent.
Explains income and demand feedbacks but underdevelops adaptation and competing policy mechanisms.
D=7, moderate confidence from introduction, contents, PW, Kirkus and reader reports. Sector cases add distinct exposure pathways; remedy advocacy is less developed.
Employment-transition questions endure; forecasts and political remedies date quickly.
Automation and institutional responses fit, although social policy is central.
Relevant entrepreneurship experience and substantive engagement from basic-income scholars and advocates.
Accessible progression from jobs to social effects to remedies.
Clear prose with overstated urgency and causal confidence.

title: Suicide of the West: How the Rebirth of Tribalism, Populism, Nationalism, and Identity Politics Is Destroying American Democracy
author: Jonah Goldberg
note: Mandatory Karpathy coverage; distinct from James Burnham's same-title book. Political and intellectual history passes hard exclusions. Anheier criticizes shallow explanatory breadth; Ceaser recognizes substantial scholarly discussion, and Wolpe identifies both acute observations and major disputes. The inspected evidence supports severe score limits but not a high-confidence foundational veto. Defense of liberalism is not itself V2 or V6; critique extends to right-wing tribalism as well. Religious language is not the main purpose, so V5/V8 do not automatically apply. US political diagnosis dominates both thematic deductions. Not selected.
notes: Selective intellectual history and weakly demonstrated links between gratitude, tribalism and prosperity.
Connects culture, institutions, economics and political identity, with loose integration.
Some useful cautions about institutional fragility, but limited actionable transfer.
Explanatory labels often substitute for tested causal chains.
D=6, moderate confidence from Ceaser, Wolpe and readers. Historical distinctions add learning; tangents and recurring decline framing have lower yield.
Institutional questions persist, but contemporary partisan examples date.
Power and institutions fit partly; little industrial or technical mechanism.
Well-read commentator with serious but sharply mixed critical reception.
Wide scope without consistently clear argumentative structure.
Fluent and witty, but rhetorical contrasts reduce conceptual precision.

title: U.S. History For Dummies
author: Steve Wiegand
note: Mandatory Karpathy coverage. General adult historical survey, not a technical curriculum and not primarily precollege despite student usefulness. H3/H5 do not follow from the Dummies label. The publisher's narrative sample explains institutional reactions and constraints, so the evidence does not establish a serious V3 failure; limited transfer is scored down. US history and political events dominate both thematic deductions. Assessment uses fourth-edition scope through 2018; original 2001 remains the P14 year. Not selected.
notes: Conventional historical survey, with limited sourcing established from inspected material.
Some links between institutions, economic development and wars, mostly chronological.
Basic context has limited transfer beyond its national setting.
Explains some responses and consequences but is primarily a survey.
D=6, low confidence from publisher sample, contents and reader reports. Numerous events add factual knowledge; simplified lists give less explanatory depth.
Broad historical background persists, though later editions extend the endpoint.
Industry appears among mostly national political and social history.
Experienced journalist and history writer; specialist validation not established.
Plain, accessible sections and memorable explanations.
Simple prose, with occasional compression of complex disputes.
